trustHistory.barrier: Fear that card numbers would be stolen in transit over the open internet
trustHistory.whatResolvedIt: Encryption standards: Netscape SSL 2.0 shipped publicly in early 1995 (SSL 3.0 1996; TLS 1999), giving browsers a visible 'secure' signal

Statutory cap: Fair Credit Billing Act (1974, amending TILA 1968) / 15 U.S.C. §1643 limits credit-card liability for unauthorized use to $50; card networks then removed even the $50 (Visa at start of 2000, MasterCard May 2000, per contemporaneous coverage) — explicitly to ease online-fraud worries
trustHistory.note: Brief suggested Mastercard ~1997; contemporaneous CNN/Bankrate (June 2000) says Visa first (early 2000), MasterCard followed May 2000. Earlier voluntary policies may exist but were not verified.

trustHistory.barrier: Perceived vs actual fraud risk (worry far exceeded incidence)
trustHistory.whatResolvedIt: Experience and time: Pew found only ~3% of internet users had a card number stolen online (2000) while ~74% of non-buyers of online gifts cited card-security worries (2001); the gap closed as users gained tenure (newcomers 50% 'very concerned' about internet crime vs veterans 29%, Feb 2001)
3-D Secure (Verified by Visa, 2001; Mastercard SecureCode) shifted liability; later EU PSD2 strong customer authentication (from Sept 2019) mandated 2FA for most remote payments
trustHistory.note: Dates from prior knowledge; not re-verified this session.

trustHistory.barrier: Trust among strangers on marketplaces (will the seller ship?)
trustHistory.whatResolvedIt: Reputation systems: eBay Feedback; Resnick & Zeckhauser (1999 data) found feedback was left >50% of the time, overwhelmingly positive, and predictive of future performance
Customer reviews: purchase likelihood for a product with 5 reviews is 270% greater than with none; verified-buyer reviews add ~15%

trustHistory.barrier: Buyer–seller payment trust in China (no card culture, weak enforcement)
trustHistory.whatResolvedIt: Escrow: Alipay held buyer funds until buyer confirmed receipt, then released to seller; credited with enabling Taobao's scale
trustHistory.date: 2003 (escrow on Taobao) / 2004 (Alipay as standalone) — sources conflict

trustHistory.barrier: Indian consumers unwilling/unable to prepay online
trustHistory.whatResolvedIt: Cash on delivery (Flipkart 2010); COD was ~60–75% of orders by 2017 and >65% of payments per a 2020 CMS study; prepaid share rose to ~41% in 2025 as UPI matured

trustHistory.barrier: Fit and 'wrong item' risk in apparel/footwear
trustHistory.whatResolvedIt: Free shipping both ways and generous return windows (Zappos treated return shipping as a marketing cost; 365-day window widely cited though current official page says 60 days — conflict)
Stored credentials: Amazon 1-Click (filed 1997, US patent granted 1999, expired 12 Sept 2017) — the first mainstream 'standing delegation' of payment authority to a merchant

Subscriptions (Subscribe & Save) and device-initiated replenishment (Dash Replenishment, 2015). The physical Dash Button (2015) was retired in 2019 in favour of virtual reordering — a lesson that the mandate, not the gadget, carries value

trustHistory.barrier: Blind purchasing via a new interface (cannot see what you are buying)
trustHistory.whatResolvedIt: Unresolved — voice commerce stalled: ~2% of Alexa owners bought by voice in 2018 and ~90% did not repeat (insider data, disputed). Cautionary analogue for agentic checkout without visual confirmation

ladder.name: Awareness
ladder.definition: Consumer knows AI agents can help with shopping and has formed an attitude (excitement vs concern).
ladder.ecomEquivalent: Mid-1990s: awareness of the web and 'online shopping' before any purchase; Pew-era surveys of internet users who had never bought online.
ladder.evidence: US: 50% more concerned than excited about AI in daily life (Pew, June 2025, up from 37% in 2021). Expectation is high: 81% expect to use agentic AI in shopping (BCG, 2025); 62% of US shoppers expect to use an AI shopping agent within two years (PYMNTS/Visa 2026).

ladder.name: Assistance
ladder.definition: AI answers questions and summarises information; the human does all searching, choosing and buying.
ladder.ecomEquivalent: Late-1990s web browsing for information (prices, specs, store hours) with offline purchase — 'research online, buy offline'.
ladder.evidence: 53% of consumers across 11 markets used AI for shopping in the past 3 months (US 48%) (McKinsey, June 2026); 73% use AI somewhere in the journey (Riskified, 2025).

ladder.name: Recommendation
ladder.definition: AI proposes specific products or merchants; the human chooses.
ladder.ecomEquivalent: Reviews, comparison-shopping engines and Amazon recommendations (late 1990s–2000s); reviews raised purchase likelihood 270% at 5 reviews.
ladder.evidence: AI-referred retail traffic +693% YoY in holiday 2025 and converting 31% better than other traffic (Adobe, measured); AI & agents influenced ~20% of Cyber Week 2025 orders (Salesforce, measured, broad definition).

ladder.name: Preparation
ladder.definition: AI assembles a cart, fills forms or builds an itinerary; the human reviews and pays.
ladder.ecomEquivalent: Saved carts and wish lists; travel sites assembling flight+hotel packages for human checkout.
ladder.evidence: 32% would let an agent decide what to buy if they still make the payment (Accenture 2026); ~60% of US shoppers would let an agent split a basket across retailers in ≥1 category (Accenture).

ladder.name: Supervised execution
ladder.definition: AI executes the purchase but the human approves each transaction (explicit confirmation step).
ladder.ecomEquivalent: Entering card details at checkout once SSL + $50/zero liability made it safe; 3-D Secure/SCA step-up confirmation.
ladder.evidence: 38% of US adults comfortable with AI completing a purchase, yet 60% would not allow any spend without approval (Visa, Feb 2026); 59% want to approve every agent clothing purchase (Worldpay 2026); 24% comfortable completing purchases today (Bain, Mar 2025).

ladder.name: Bounded autonomy
ladder.definition: AI buys without per-transaction approval inside explicit limits (amount, category, merchant list, time window).
ladder.ecomEquivalent: Stored credentials (1-Click, 1999) and merchant-initiated card-on-file payments; in India, RBI e-mandates with AFA exemption below a threshold.
ladder.evidence: 9% would let agents initiate and complete purchases within defined boundaries (Accenture); comfort falls from 29% 'very comfortable' at ≤$20 to 6% at ≥$500 (Wildfire 2026); 69% would allow up to $100 on groceries/essentials (Global Payments, May 2026).

ladder.name: Persistent delegation
ladder.definition: Standing mandate: AI monitors needs and replenishes or rebooks continuously, reporting by exception.
ladder.ecomEquivalent: Subscribe & Save, Dash Replenishment (2015), pet-food autoship; Pix Automático (2025) in Brazil as a payments-rail analogue.
ladder.evidence: Consumers expect agents to make 15% of their purchases within five years (up from 9% a year earlier; Global Payments 2026). Historical caution: Dash Button retired 2019; voice ordering ~2% adoption in 2018.

scenarios.name: Weekly grocery shopping
scenarios.why: High frequency and stable lists favour delegation, and grocery is the top category for stated willingness (41% Checkout.com 2026; 34% Doss; 69% would allow up to $100 on groceries/essentials). But substitutions, freshness and delivery-slot trade-offs mean a weekly basket should be agent-built and human-approved. Staple sub-baskets can move to bounded autonomy.
risks: Unwanted substitutions or poor-quality fresh produce
Basket inflation or upsell bias toward sponsored items
Delivery-slot failure and perishables left unattended
scenarios.commercial: The fight moves from shelf placement to the agent's default list: incumbents with loyalty data and slot capacity can lock in the basket. Retail media must be machine-readable; price-match logic compresses margins on known-value items.

scenarios.name: Household-supplies replenishment
scenarios.why: Standardised, low-ticket, low-emotion, repeat SKUs: the clearest case for an automation curve, and the historical precedent is subscriptions/autoship. Limits (per-order cap, approved brands) contain the downside. 31% would delegate household supplies (Checkout.com); 23% 'very comfortable' for toiletries/home goods vs 17% for travel (Wildfire).
scenarios.commercial: Brand loyalty becomes the agent's default; incumbents win if they are the starting SKU, while challengers must win on price or spec in agent-readable feeds. Subscribe-style discounts become the price of entry.

scenarios.name: Buying headphones
scenarios.why: Highly comparable specs and transparent prices make agent research and shortlisting valuable (CE online penetration roughly half of category sales per eMarketer-derived estimates). But fit, sound preference and mid-range ticket make human approval of the final pick sensible.
risks: Return friction if fit or comfort is wrong
Agent optimising price over the user's real preference
scenarios.commercial: Brands must compete on structured specs, verified reviews and warranty terms visible to agents. Marketplaces with authenticity guarantees and easy returns gain share; the value of display ads shrinks.

scenarios.name: Booking family travel
scenarios.why: Agents help most with multi-constraint search (dates, budget, kids' needs), and travel research via AI is common (58% in one vendor survey). But checkout delegation is low (≈6% per FirstPage; 17% 'very comfortable' for airline/hotels per Wildfire), cancellation rules are complex and stakes are high, so humans should approve the itinerary.
scenarios.commercial: OTAs and airlines with API-accessible inventory and clear fare rules gain. Supplier-direct may regain share if agents query suppliers directly. Expect disintermediation pressure on meta-search advertising.

scenarios.name: Luxury handbag
scenarios.why: Emotional, identity-laden purchase with controlled pricing and authentication risk. Delegation willingness falls steeply with ticket size (6% very comfortable at ≥$500). The agent's role is discovery, availability and authenticity checks, not buying.
risks: Loss of the brand experience and clienteling relationship
scenarios.commercial: Luxury houses will gate agent access (no structured price feeds, appointment-only) to protect scarcity; secondary/resale platforms may embrace agents first. The relationship asset (clienteling) becomes a moat.

scenarios.name: Buying a car
scenarios.why: Highest ticket and long cycle, with financing, trade-in, test drive and (in the US) dealer-franchise channel constraints. Agents add value in comparison, inventory search and price negotiation prep; completion stays human and in-person. Comfort at ≥$500 is just 6% (Wildfire).
risks: Identity and fraud exposure on large transfers
scenarios.commercial: Agent-to-dealer negotiation could compress dealer gross margins and raise price transparency. OEM direct models and digital retailers benefit; lead-gen marketplaces face disintermediation.

scenarios.name: Enterprise software purchase
scenarios.why: Procurement is already rule-bound (budgets, approved vendors, security reviews), which gives an agent a natural mandate. But contracts are bespoke, multi-stakeholder and multi-year, so agents should prepare RFPs and comparisons, negotiate within guardrails, and route signature to humans. 53% of US business decision-makers would let AI agents negotiate prices/terms with other AI agents (Visa B2AI).
scenarios.commercial: Vendors need machine-readable pricing, security documentation and trial provisioning. Opaque 'contact sales' pricing becomes a liability; procurement platforms become agent orchestration layers.

regions.howEcomDeveloped: Desktop-era, card-based, search-led. The trust stack (FCBA liability cap, network zero-liability, SSL, reviews) was in place before mass adoption. Amazon's stored credentials and Prime shipping made card-on-file the norm. Penetration grew steadily, jumped in 2020, and in 2026 still sits below a fifth of retail.

hypotheses.text: The US will lead in agent-executed checkout volume because card-on-file and zero-liability already allocate fraud risk away from consumers, and the major agent platforms and protocols are US-based.
hypotheses.for: Liability regime predates agents; OpenAI/Google/Visa/Mastercard/Amazon launches are US-first; MS forecasts $190–385bn by 2030.
hypotheses.against: US consumers are more concerned about AI than the global median (Pew 50% vs 34%); US AI-shopping use (48%) is below McKinsey's 11-market average; stated autonomy is just 6–10% in several US surveys.

hypotheses.text: Agentic adoption will follow the e-commerce pattern of low-regret categories first (household, grocery staples), then spread up the ticket ladder.
hypotheses.for: Category data (Checkout, Doss, Wildfire ticket thresholds, Bain's note that actual AI purchases are small-ticket).
hypotheses.against: McKinsey shows apparel (not grocery) had the largest 2026 gain in AI-completed purchases; grocery delivery economics may cap execution.

hypotheses.text: Trust will attach to payment brands rather than AI labs.
hypotheses.for: Bain: 39% more comfortable with a familiar payment provider; PYMNTS: banks, wallets and networks most trusted; Visa: payment-network AI 35% vs independent agents 28%.
hypotheses.against: Bain: only 16% more comfortable with their bank or card issuer, so trust is brand-specific, not sector-wide.

regions.howEcomDeveloped: Leapfrogged cards: marketplace-first (Taobao/Tmall, JD), escrow and super-app wallets, then mobile-first and livestream/social commerce. The trust problem was solved by the platform (escrow) rather than the state, and penetration passed a quarter of retail.

hypotheses.text: Agentic commerce in China will be platform-internal (inside super-apps that own the wallet, catalogue and logistics) rather than open-protocol.
hypotheses.for: Alipay/Taobao vertical integration; Qwen-in-app agent integration; Alibaba's history of closing trust gaps in-house.
hypotheses.against: Platform rivalry (Alibaba vs Tencent vs ByteDance vs Meituan) restricts cross-platform access, limiting what any one agent can compare.

hypotheses.text: Regulatory labelling and algorithm rules will shape agent disclosure more than payment rules will.
hypotheses.for: CAC GenAI measures and labelling rules (prior knowledge).
hypotheses.against: No evidence found this session of China-specific rules on agent-initiated payments; unverified.

regions.name: India

ecomHistory.metric: COD share of online orders 60–75% (industry estimates) — payments-mix indicator, not penetration
Prepaid share of e-commerce orders 41% (from 32% a year earlier)

indicators.label: E-commerce share of retail
indicators.value: Not verified this session (Bain/Flipkart 'How India Shops Online' and Redseer are the sources to use)

indicators.label: UPI scale
indicators.value: ~185.8bn transactions in FY2024-25; monthly volume passed ~20bn in Aug 2025

indicators.label: Delegated-payment regulation
indicators.value: RBI e-mandate framework: additional factor of authentication (AFA) exempt for recurring debits up to ₹15,000 (₹1 lakh for select categories), with pre-debit notification

indicators.label: Agentic pilots
indicators.value: NPCI, Razorpay and OpenAI announced a UPI agentic-payments pilot in ChatGPT (Oct 2025)

regions.howEcomDeveloped: Mobile-first and COD-led through the 2010s. Demonetisation (2016) and UPI (2016 onward) shifted the payment mix toward prepaid, and the shopper base expanded to Tier-2+ cities via Flipkart, Amazon, Meesho and quick commerce.

hypotheses.text: India's public rails (UPI + e-mandate caps) give it the most explicit regulatory template for bounded autonomy: limits per mandate rather than per-transaction approval.
hypotheses.for: The RBI e-mandate AFA threshold already creates 'bounded autonomy'; the NPCI agentic pilot.
hypotheses.against: COD persistence shows consumers prefer to verify goods before paying, which is the opposite of delegation; a 41% prepaid share means most orders are still COD.

hypotheses.text: Quick-commerce grocery will be the first mass agentic use case.
hypotheses.for: High-frequency staples and app-based ordering; global evidence that grocery is the most-delegable category.
hypotheses.against: No India-specific delegation survey was found this session.

regions.name: Japan

ecomHistory.metric: BtoC EC rate for goods (METI e-commerce market survey)

indicators.label: Cashless payment ratio
indicators.value: 42.8% in 2024 (METI), passing the government's 40% target

indicators.label: Agent/AI attitude data
indicators.value: No Japan-specific agentic delegation survey found this session

regions.howEcomDeveloped: Dense convenience-store and physical-retail network, and cash-heavy until the 2019 cashless push. E-commerce grew through marketplaces (Rakuten, Amazon Japan, Yahoo/LY), with konbini payment and pickup as trust devices. Goods EC rate stayed below 10%.

hypotheses.text: Japan will adopt agentic commerce slowly in goods but faster in replenishment via existing loyalty/point ecosystems.
hypotheses.for: Low goods EC rate; strong points ecosystems (prior knowledge).
hypotheses.against: No direct survey evidence found; this hypothesis is speculative.

hypotheses.text: Physical retail density lowers the convenience gain from delegation.
hypotheses.for: Dense konbini network; EC rate below 10%.
hypotheses.against: Ageing population could raise demand for delegated replenishment (no evidence retrieved).

regions.name: Southeast Asia

ecomHistory.metric: e-commerce GMV ~US$159bn (e-Conomy SEA 2024) — GMV, not a % of retail

indicators.label: Marketplace concentration
indicators.value: Shopee-led, with Lazada, TikTok Shop/Tokopedia; shares not verified this session

indicators.label: Payments

indicators.label: Consumer openness
indicators.value: Singapore is in the Worldpay/Global Payments 7-market panel; Accenture's APAC cut reports higher trust than global (85% vs 74%, conflicting definitions)

regions.howEcomDeveloped: Mobile-first, marketplace-plus-social-commerce growth; super-apps (Grab, GoTo) bundle payments and delivery. Fragmented across six-plus regulatory regimes.

hypotheses.text: Social-commerce-native markets will adopt conversational agents faster than search-native markets.
hypotheses.for: APAC trust figures in Accenture coverage are higher than global.
hypotheses.against: APAC figures conflict (85% vs 74%) and lack country splits; evidence is thin.

hypotheses.text: Fragmented payment rails will slow cross-border agent checkout.
hypotheses.for: Each market has its own QR scheme.
hypotheses.against: Regional QR interoperability links are expanding (prior knowledge; not verified).

regions.name: Europe (EU/UK)

ecomHistory.metric: UK internet sales % of retail peaked during Jan 2021 lockdown (ONS J4MC; ~high-30s%)
EU: roughly three-quarters of internet users bought online in past 12 months (Eurostat)

indicators.label: Delegated-payment regime
indicators.value: PSD2 strong customer authentication (from Sep 2019) requires 2FA for customer-initiated remote payments; merchant-initiated transactions and low-value exemptions are the main paths for agent payments; PSD3/PSR in progress

indicators.label: AI regulation
indicators.value: EU AI Act in force Aug 2024; GPAI obligations from Aug 2025; transparency duties relevant to shopping agents

indicators.label: UK trust
indicators.value: 24% of UK online adults trust agents with routine purchases (Forrester, Mar 2025); 37% of UK say never delegate vs 24% across 6 markets (Checkout.com 2026); 40% would let agents handle routine tasks (Checkout.com, Sep 2025)

indicators.label: Card-not-present fraud history
indicators.value: SCA introduced as a regulatory answer to CNP fraud

regions.howEcomDeveloped: Card plus local schemes (iDEAL, Bancontact, Swish, etc.) with strong consumer-protection law (14-day withdrawal right). The UK has one of the highest online shares of retail globally; the continent is more heterogeneous.

hypotheses.text: SCA makes 'bounded autonomy' harder in the EU than in the US unless agents run under merchant-initiated or delegated-authentication frameworks.
hypotheses.for: The PSD2 RTS design requires per-transaction authentication for customer-initiated payments.
hypotheses.against: Delegated authentication and token-based agent credentials (network tokens) may satisfy SCA; PSD3 outcomes are unsettled.

hypotheses.text: UK consumers are notably more resistant to delegation than other markets.
hypotheses.against: The same vendor's 2025 UK study found 40% open to routine-task delegation, so wording matters.

hypotheses.text: EU AI Act transparency and consumer law will push agent disclosure (sponsored ranking, reasoning) to become standard.
hypotheses.for: Capgemini: two-thirds trust AI more when it explains its reasoning; 76% want clear rules for when an assistant acts.
hypotheses.against: Act obligations for most shopping agents are light (not high-risk); enforcement timelines may slip.

indicators.value: AMVO online-sales data not retrieved this session

hypotheses.text: Brazil's Pix Automático provides a regulator-built mandate rail that could carry bounded-autonomy agent payments.

hypotheses.against: No evidence yet of agent-initiated Pix; payment-fraud concerns in Brazil are high (not quantified here).

conflicts: Autonomous-purchase willingness ranges from 6% (Worldpay 2025 US; Doss) to 9% (Accenture), 10% (NMI; Mastercard), 21% (Worldpay clothing), 27% (Visa 'without limits'), 30% (Contentsquare), 33% (Mastercard ≤$1,000) and 70% 'at least somewhat comfortable' (Riskified 2025). Wording (autonomy vs approval, 'at least somewhat', category or limit qualifiers) drives most of the spread; do not average.
Within the Visa B2AI survey, 27% are comfortable with AI spending 'without limits' but 60% would not allow any spend without approval. These sum to <100% but suggest different question framings.
Worldpay 2026 report sample: >16,000 consumers in 7 markets (FashionUnited) vs 8,000 (Worldpay's own page).
Accenture 2026: 74% would trust an AI agent more than their best friend (global) vs 85% (APAC coverage); sample reported as ~25,000 and 25,590.

Travel openness: Worldpay coverage (via aggregator) calls travel among the most open categories, while PYMNTS coverage of Worldpay lists travel among the less likely; FirstPage (6.3% checkout) and Wildfire (17% vs 23% household) support lower.
Riskified: 70% at least somewhat comfortable (Q4 2025, multi-market) vs 55% NOT comfortable (Q1 2026, US/UK) — different samples, so not a clean trend.
Card-network zero liability: the brief cited Mastercard ~1997; contemporaneous coverage (CNN/Bankrate, June 2000) says Visa dropped the $50 at the start of 2000 and MasterCard followed in May 2000.
Alipay launch: 2003 (escrow on Taobao) vs 2004 (standalone Alipay) in different sources.
Zappos returns: 365-day window widely cited vs 60 days on the current official policy page.
US 2010 e-commerce share: 4.4% (Haver, Census-based) vs 6.4% (Digital Commerce 360, different method); 4.2% not found.
Salesforce Cyber Week 2025: $73bn/22% forecast vs $67bn/~20% actual 'AI-influenced'. 'Influenced' is far broader than agent-executed.
Alexa 2018 voice purchases: ~2% (The Information insider data) vs 26.1% of smart-speaker owners (Voicebot survey); Amazon disputed the 2%.
Mastercard teen survey footprint: 13 vs 16 countries.
gaps: Network policy blocked direct page fetches (WebFetch/curl) for nearly all hosts, and the shared web-search budget ran out mid-research. All 'search-confirmed' figures come from search-result extracts, not full documents; question wording and denominators are often missing.

Items tagged verification='prior-knowledge' (China NBS shares, Japan METI EC rates, UPI volumes, RBI thresholds, Pix Automático, EU AI Act/PSD2 dates, agentic launch dates, Chewy Autoship share) were NOT re-verified this session and must be checked before publication.

No category-level US e-commerce penetration verified for travel, household CPG, beauty, furniture, autos, luxury, pet, pharmacy, food delivery, financial products or B2B. Only 5 eMarketer-derived values were seen (secondary).
No country-level splits retrieved for China, India, Japan or Southeast Asia from the multi-country agent surveys (Accenture, Worldpay/Global Payments, McKinsey, Capgemini).
Income splits are largely absent; age splits are limited to Gen Z vs Boomers (Visa), Gen Z (PYMNTS) and teens (Mastercard).
